extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent attorneys, and law students studying patent pleading practice
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards for when and how a defendant must give notice of special defenses in patent infringement litigation (what defenses require notice, what the notice must contain, timing, form, and related pleading practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defenses available under the general issue without notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the ordinary defences open to defendants in infringement actions, nineteen may be set up and proved under the general issue, without notice or special plea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerated examples given in the text (as stated): (1) the alleged invention is not the product of inventive skill; (2) it does not fall within either of the protected classes of inventions; (3) it is not useful; (4) no such patent as the one declared upon has ever existed; (5) the plaintiff's patent was issued contrary to law; (6) the invention described in the patent is neither an art, a machine, a manufacture, a composition of matter, a design, or an improvement; (7) the specification is ambiguous; (8) the claim is excessive and has not been cured within reasonable time by a disclaimer; (9) the claim is ambiguous; (10) the patent in force at the date of the infringement has been surrendered; (11) the patent declared on has been repealed; (12) the plaintiff has no such title to the patent as enables him to sue at law; (13) [text numbering jumps but continues with other common defenses]; (14) that the invention practiced by the defendant is not identical with the one covered by the patent; (15) that the acts of the defendant in reference to the patented invention were not acts of making, use, or sale; (16) that the practice of the invention by the defendant occurred before the issue of the patent or after it had expired; (17) that the practice of the invention by the defendant was in pursuance of his lawful rights; (18) that the plaintiff is estopped by his own conduct from pursuing his action; (19) that the plaintiff's right of action has been released or extinguished or merged in a judgment.  (Text explains these cover most defences admissible under general issue; earlier authorities recognized slightly different scopes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific defenses that require notice (the five special matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Five defenses can be introduced under the general issue only after due notice (or else must be specially pleaded): (1) that the inventive act resulting in the invention was not performed by the patentee (surreptitiously obtained); (2) that the patentee, though a true inventor, was not the first to perform the inventive act; (3) that the patented invention is not legally new; (4) that it has been abandoned to the public; (5) that the specification fraudulently misrepresents the scope of the invention or the mode of rendering it available in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If defendant prefers he may plead specially either or all of these five defences and plead the general issue as to the others (except Statute of Limitations). When pleading specially the special pleas must possess all the requisites which the law prescribes for notices under the general issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and service of notice (general requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice must be in writing and must be complete and precise enough to answer its purpose: to secure to the plaintiff an opportunity to prepare to meet the defence and to guard against unwarrantable surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice must give the plaintiff such information as to events, persons, places, and dates as will enable him to acquaint himself with the truth of the matters alleged. The notice should be so full and particular as reasonably to answer the end in view; less is not reasonable. If the first notice is defective, another properly constructed may be substituted. The notice is not to be pleaded but must be served on the plaintiff or his attorney at least thirty days before the opening of the term at which the cause is to be tried (thirty days before the term, not merely before trial). Failure to serve such notice is good ground for continuance. The notice may be repeated if at first insufficient; it may be given without an order of court; it may be given after depositions have been taken (those depositions may then be admitted if pertinent). In equity the notice is given in the answer and may be amended under court permission (softening the strict service rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency/specificity standard for notices (sources of proof and reasonable particularity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A notice is sufficient if it indicates the sources of the defendant's proofs with such certainty that the plaintiff can resort to and identify them; the aim is to enable plaintiff to fix with precision what is relied upon and prepare to meet it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice is meant to relieve the patentee from making useless inquiries and to enable him to prepare; it is not merely to put him on inquiry. The party giving notice need not be so specific as to relieve the other from all inquiry or effort; but he must fairly put his adversary in a position to ascertain all that is necessary. A general reference to a work or volume that misleads or embarrasses the party is improper. Defective notices cannot be remedied simply by offering expert testimony that they could have found the material; the court requires particulars (pages/headings) so the patentee can turn to the article without searching the entire volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of fraudulent specification: requisites
rubrics_metrics.description: A notice alleging that the patentee's specification is fraudulent must point out the concealment or redundancy relied upon and must aver specifically that it originated in an intention to deceive the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A general statement that the specification was fraudulently made too comprehensive or too narrow is not sufficient. Alleging the Description is vague/ambiguous or contains superfluous matter, or that the Claim is frivolous, without asserting an intention to deceive, is defective. The plaintiff must be forewarned both of the particular errors in his specification and that they were committed in pursuance of a design to mislead; otherwise the notice only gives matters that could be proven under the defence of ambiguity without notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of surreptitious obtaining / prior inventor (requisites)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the defence is that the patentee surreptitiously and unjustly obtained the patent for what was in fact another's invention (who was diligently reducing it to practice), the notice must give particulars analogous to prior-knowledge/use notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice should give the name and residence of the prior inventor, the date of his conception of the idea or means, the date of its conception by the patentee, and aver that the former was employing due diligence in reducing it to practice. No allegations of fraud or wilful wrong are necessary; the defence is complete if these facts are established regardless of motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of prior patent or publication: requisites
rubrics_metrics.description: A notice of a prior patent must give the name of the patentee and the date of his patent and allege it to be prior to the date of the patent in suit. A notice of prior publication must set forth its title and date of publication, mention the particular arts or articles described which are claimed to be identical with the patented invention, and name the volume and page where the description is found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The date given for a patent or publication must not be earlier than its true issue date. The notice should specify the page or heading in a work so the patentee can find the description without searching an entire volume. A printed publication or patent not properly set out in the notice cannot be used to show prior knowledge. Defective notice of a prior publication is not aided by expert evidence that they would know where to look.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of prior use / prior knowledge: requisites
rubrics_metrics.description: When alleging prior use or knowledge as a defence to novelty, the notice must be tailored to the nature of the defence and disclose the names and residences of persons who had knowledge of or used the invention before the patentee, and the localities in which it was used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is immaterial whether the first inventor is known or unknown; the critical fact is that the invention itself was known or used before the patentee. The notice must give such detailed information as the defendant possesses and can fairly impart without prejudicing his rights so the plaintiff can identify persons and places and resort to them. The persons named are those who had the knowledge or made the use (not merely expected witnesses). The locality must be alleged with reasonable certainty (naming only a county is insufficient; naming particular towns, villages, or establishments is proper). The date of such knowledge/use need not be stated except by a general averment that it preceded the patentee's inventive act. The notice must extend to the entire invention claimed, not merely to elements. A defective notice cannot be cured by presenting the prior publication/patent/rejected application as evidence of use without proper notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of abandonment to the public: requisites
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice of abandonment differs by the form of abandonment alleged (abandonment by public use and sale versus abandonment by general conduct); the notice must reflect the nature of the evidence to be adduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For abandonment by public use or sale the notice must be sufficiently specific as other prior-use notices (naming persons/places/dates as appropriate). Abandonment by general conduct requires notice that permits the plaintiff to know the particular public conduct relied upon. Evidence of abandonment cannot be admitted without proper notice. The notice should apply to the whole invention as patented (need not specify particular portion of the patent unless appropriate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Special pleading vs general issue practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant may plead special defences specially or raise them under the general issue when permitted; but where statute prescribes a special plea (or notice) the special plea must conform to statutory requisites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a defendant pleads specially the special pleas must possess all requisites law prescribes for notices under the general issue. The law recognizes distinctions between pleadings at law and in equity: in equity the defendant must specially set forth every defence, and amendments in equity may relax strictness of timing/service for notice. Courts differ historically on whether certain matters required special pleading or could be raised under general issue without notice; modern rule (as described) identifies five categories requiring notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of defective or omitted notice
rubrics_metrics.description: If proper notice is not given, evidence supporting those special defences cannot be admitted; failure to serve notice in time is good ground for continuance; defective notice may be replaced by a proper one before trial in some circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A defective description of a publication, or failure to give required particulars (names, pages, dates, places), prevents use of that item to show prior knowledge or use. Where notice is required but not given, the defendant cannot examine witnesses on those matters; the plaintiff is entitled to a continuance if no notice or its equivalent plea or answer is filed thirty days before the term. In equity some flexibility exists by amendment of the answer.
